title: Armed With New Majorities, Democrats Target Trump's War in Iran via Power of the Purse
snippet: Capitol Hill Democrats are weighing aggressive legislative strategies—from spending cutoffs to War Powers Resolutions—to compel the Trump administration to wind down military operations against Iran.
content:
WASHINGTON — Fresh off midterms that handed them control of both the House and Senate, Democrats are preparing to use their newly acquired legislative leverage to force an end to the military conflict with Iran. But as incoming committee leaders map out their legislative playbook, a debate has emerged over how swiftly and aggressively to wield the power of the purse.

Ending the unauthorized war was a centerpiece of the Democratic pitch to voters, who have grown increasingly weary of foreign engagements that party leaders blame for driving up domestic costs. Now, lawmakers are assessing whether to attach war-related restrictions to upcoming mandatory spending packages or launch targeted War Powers Resolutions early next year.

Internal Debate Over Funding Leverage

The first major test could come ahead of a Dec. 11 government funding deadline. A coalition of progressive and moderate senators, led by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., is urging leadership to block any temporary funding bill that lacks explicit prohibitions on spending for the Iran war.

However, incoming House Appropriations Committee Chair Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., and incoming House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., have expressed caution about using a stopgap measure as leverage if it risks a government shutdown. While DeLauro has signaled support for eventual funding cutoffs, she told reporters that the public does not believe "shutting the government down ends the war."

Meeks echoed that sentiment, emphasizing that while he plans to introduce a War Powers Resolution in January to curb military action and demand real diplomatic engagement, triggering a partial shutdown would only harm working Americans relying on federal services.

War Powers and Veto Battles

Once Democrats officially take control in January, party leaders plan to deploy multiple legislative mechanisms. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries indicated that lawmakers intend to pass a binding War Powers Resolution and send it directly to President Trump's desk, putting the administration on the spot.

"There's nothing more powerful than putting that bill on the president's desk," Jeffries said, pointing out that the conflict remains broadly unpopular across the country.

Democrats could also attach anti-war provisions to the fiscal year 2028 appropriations bills, the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), or an impending debt ceiling extension. Historical precedents exist: in 1973, Congress successfully cut off funding for combat activities in Southeast Asia, compelling President Richard Nixon to sign the restriction into law.

Constitutional Obstacles Ahead

Despite the planned push, forcing a commander-in-chief to cease military operations presents significant legal and political hurdles. President Trump has asserted broad authority under Article II of the Constitution to conduct operations without prior congressional authorization, while brushing off previous non-binding war powers votes as unconstitutional.

A White House official dismissed the Democrats' maneuvers, stating that the administration's economic pressure campaign is already constraining Iran to the point where major combat operations are unnecessary, calling the legislative push a form of baseless obstruction.

Legal scholars warn that enforcing a funding ban could trigger complex constitutional questions, particularly regarding defensive actions, port blockades, and protecting U.S. vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. Incoming House Armed Services Committee Chair Adam Smith, D-Wash., acknowledged that navigating legal loopholes and potential executive non-compliance will place Congress in "uncharted territory," emphasizing that reining in the executive branch will require sustained political fighting in the months ahead.
